From ute (“outside, outdoors”) + pils (“pilsner, beer”), literally “outdoor beer”. The second element pils (“pilsner, beer”) is a shortening of pilsner (“pilsner”).
First attested in 1963, in the phrase vårens første utepils (“the first outdoor beer of spring”) in Arbeiderbladet. The association with the first beer drunk outdoors in spring is therefore already present in the earliest known written attestation. The word was first included as a dictionary headword in the 1996 edition of Tanums store rettskrivningsordbok, and was added to Bokmålsordboka and Nynorskordboka in 2020.

1000035.etyen:
Internationalism, based on Portuguese Angola, from Kimbundu ngola (“king of Ndongo; royal title”). The title has been connected with ngolo (“resistance, strength, vigor”), in the same word family as kukola (“to endure; to be firm or solid”), although the precise historical formation is uncertain. The title was borne by rulers of the kingdom of Ndongo and was interpreted by the Portuguese as the name of the territory.
Parallel international adaptations include Norwegian Nynorsk Angola, Danish Angola, Swedish Angola, German Angola, Dutch Angola and English Angola.

1000291.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse Andreas, from Latin Andreas, ultimately from Ancient Greek Ἀνδρέᾱς (Andréās). The Greek name belongs to the word family of ἀνήρ (anḗr, “man”), genitive ἀνδρός (andrós), and ἀνδρεῖος (andreîos, “manly, brave”), and may originally have been a short form of compound names beginning in Andro-. The name spread through the veneration of Andrew the Apostle. Doublet of Anders and André. First attested in the 12th century in Norway.
Cognate with Danish Andreas, Swedish Andreas, Icelandic Andreas, Faroese Andrias, German Andreas, Dutch Andreas and English Andrew. Doublet of Ande

1000547.etyen:
Internationalism, based on Latin Mercurius (“Mercury, the Roman god; the planet Mercury”). The Norwegian form is a shortened adaptation of the Latin name, with final -ius omitted. The Latin name itself is of uncertain origin, possibly connected with merx (“merchandise, goods”), or perhaps ultimately from Etruscan and subsequently influenced by Latin merx.
The astronomical sense is named after the Roman deity. The association reflects Mercury's traditional swiftness; the planet moves around the Sun faster than any other planet, completing an orbit in about 88 Earth days.

en.g: a female given name from German [in turn from Old High German, in turn from Proto-Germanic], equivalent to English Gertrude, originally a short form of names ending in -trud, especially Gjertrud

1001315.etyen:
Possibly borrowed from German Trude, a short form of names ending in -trud, especially Gertrud. The element -trud is from Proto-Germanic *þrūþiz (“strength”), from *þrewwaną (“to grow, thrive”) + *-þiz (“abstract noun suffix”). In Gjertrud, the first element is ultimately from Old High German gēr (“spear”). Alternatively, the Scandinavian name may in some cases represent a variant of Trud, from Old Norse Þrúðr, from the same Proto-Germanic element.
Compare German Trude, English Trudy, Danish Gertrud, Swedish Gertrud, Estonian Kertu and Icelandic Þrúður.

1001571.etyen:

Compare Danish Magnar, Swedish Magnar and Faroese Magnar (“male given name”).

1005155.etyen:
From the name of the farm Fornebo, recorded as Forneboo in 1557. The name is of Old Norse origin, but its precise formation is uncertain: the first element may be the personal name Forni or forn (“old”), and the second may be bú (“dwelling, farm”) or búð (“booth, hut”).
Rygh favours the interpretation involving búð and suggests that the name may refer to huts used for salt boiling.
